section.title: The definite integral
section.p: Sigma notation made rectangular sums readable. Now we give the limiting process a name.
The definite integral is the number that rectangular sums approach when every rectangle becomes thin.
This definition is the formal version of the accumulation idea that began the chapter.

exercise.title: Why do we need partitions and sample points?

statement.p: A partition cuts [a,b] into subintervals; a sample point chooses a height on each piece. In your own words, why is a Riemann sum more general than equal-width left or right sums, and why are equal widths a convenience rather than a requirement?

hint.p: The integral should belong to the function and the interval, not to one particular way of chopping. Unequal widths are allowed as long as every piece becomes thin.

exercise.title: Why is the definite integral the common limit of all fine Riemann sums?

statement.p: The definition asks that the sums approach one number as the mesh of the partition goes to zero, no matter how partitions and sample points are chosen. In your own words, why is that stronger than the convergence of one special sum, and what do the symbols \int, f(x), and dx remember from the rectangles?

hint.p: \int is an elongated S for sum, f(x) is the height, and dx is the descendant of the small width. The integral is what those approximations approach.

subsection.title: Why the sample point should not matter
subsection.p: The definition of the integral asks for more than the convergence of one special sum. It asks that all sufficiently fine Riemann sums approach the same number.
Why such a strong requirement?
Because the integral should belong to the function and the interval, not to our particular choice of sample points.

For a smooth graph, this is natural. If a subinterval is very narrow, the values of f inside it are close to one another. A left endpoint, a right endpoint, and a midpoint give nearly the same height. The rectangle heights may differ a little, but the differences become negligible as the widths shrink.

exercise.title: Why should the sample point not matter for a well-behaved function?

statement.p: On a very narrow subinterval, the values of a continuous function stay close together. In your own words, why do left, right, and midpoint heights then become interchangeable, and why does that force all fine rectangular sums toward one number?

hint.p: When all fine rectangular sums are forced toward one number, that number is the integral. The sample choice is a finite-sum detail that the limit is trying to erase.

subsection.title: Integrability, informally first
subsection.p: The definition says:
subsection.md: \text{all fine Riemann sums must approach one common value.}
subsection.p: This is a strong condition, but most functions we meet in first-year calculus satisfy it.

statement.p: If f is continuous on [a,b], then f is integrable on [a,b].

subsection.p: We will discuss this more carefully later. The intuition is that a continuous function cannot jump wildly inside tiny intervals. When the subintervals are small, the function values inside each subinterval are forced to stay close together.
Continuity is not required, though. A function with a finite number of jump discontinuities can still be integrable.
For example, the step function
is integrable on [0,2]. The jump at x=1 affects only one point. Riemann sums still settle down to the total area:
But not every bounded function is integrable.

note.title: Moral
note.p: The definite integral is not just any limit of convenient sums. It exists only when fine Riemann sums are forced toward the same value, regardless of the sample points.

paragraphs.p: This warning is not meant to frighten us. It tells us why the definition is honest. The continuous functions, piecewise continuous functions, and ordinary models of science and geometry are integrable. But the definition knows how to reject functions that oscillate too violently at every scale.
We now have the central object of integral calculus:

When f\ge0, it is area under the graph. But the original motivation came from velocity, and velocity can be negative. The next step is to understand the integral as signed accumulation: area above the axis counts positively, area below the axis counts negatively.

exercise.title: Why can a bounded function fail to be integrable?

statement.p: Continuity on a closed interval is enough for integrability, and a finite number of jumps can still be all right. In your own words, why is boundedness not enough by itself, and what goes wrong if a function oscillates too violently at every scale?

hint.p: Integrability asks that all fine Riemann sums settle on one value. If heights refuse to settle inside every tiny interval, the sums cannot agree.
